messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas, a 68-year-old psychologist, presented as a man holding himself together with immense, exhausting effort. He spoke in measured tones, his clinical vocabulary a thin shield against the disarray he described. It was his wife who had finally insisted he seek help, after finding him awake for the third consecutive night, sitting rigidly in a chair facing the bedroom door. The trauma occurred two years prior, during the final, violent months of his previous marriage. His ex-wife, whose rage had been escalating for years, attacked him during a bike ride on a crowded public greenway. She had screamed at him, shoved him from his bicycle into the path of onlookers, and struck him repeatedly while he was on the ground. The public humiliation was as searing as the physical blows.

In the aftermath, the memory of the event refused to cohere. Thomas reported that he could not construct a linear story of what happened, a fact that tormented him as a professional dedicated to narrative. Instead, the trauma lived in him as a series of stark, silent photographs: the mangled front wheel of his bicycle, his ex-wife's face contorted in fury, the astonished faces in the crowd. These frozen images would flash into his mind without warning, so vivid they felt like a present-tense reality, plunging him back into a state of immediate physical danger. At other times, he would be overwhelmed by a wave of pure terror and shame, a full-body emotional echo of the event, but with no accompanying image at all. This fragmented recall served as constant, painful proof of his own failings; he had come to believe he was fundamentally inadequate, a man who couldn't even make sense of his own mind.

This conviction of his own inadequacy, coupled with the new certainty that people are not what they seem, has left him feeling perpetually unsafe. His belief that the world’s apparent order had been destroyed meant that threat could emerge from anywhere. This pervasive sense of danger dictated his movements and choices. He began watching his colleagues and students closely, scanning their faces for the subtle signs of a turn, the first hint of betrayal he was sure he had missed before. At night, this vigilance became all-consuming; he found it almost impossible to feel safe after dark and would often wake suddenly, his first instinct to check the locks and windows. On these nights, when the threat felt most imminent, the memory was hardest to keep at bay; the stark image of his ex-wife's face would often surface in the dark, pulled into the present by his fear. The hypervigilance made his world dense with potential threats, so that even the distant glint of chrome on a bicycle handlebar across the university campus could snag his attention and cause a surge of adrenaline.

Triggers are now embedded in the fabric of his professional and personal life. Seeing a bicycle can leave him breathless. Being in crowded spaces, like the university quad between classes, feels intolerably dangerous. Most difficult, however, is being alone with women. This has made his work a minefield. During one-on-one meetings with his female graduate students, he is overcome with the conviction that he is in danger, that their benign professional manner is a mask. This visceral reaction in the safety of his own office served as fresh, irrefutable proof of his core belief: he was fundamentally broken, unable to function in the most basic professional scenarios. This perception immediately forces him into a state of rigid, forced composure. He focuses on controlling his emotions absolutely, believing any show of fear or anger would confirm his weakness. He has also stopped wearing his favourite flannel shirts, as his ex-wife was wearing one that day, and he avoids them as if the fabric itself were contaminated. This act of avoidance, however, had the unintended effect of making the shirts even more potent as a trigger; now, even seeing one in a shop window served as a stark, visceral reminder of the attack.

The strategies he uses to manage this constant sense of threat have only tightened the trap. His relentless effort to suppress all emotion seems to have further fractured the trauma memory; the more he pushes the feelings down, the more the event dissolves into those disconnected, terrifying snapshots. This, in turn, reinforces his belief that he is broken. The feeling of being constantly on guard has also cemented his negative appraisals; if the world requires this much vigilance, his conclusion that it is a treacherous place must be correct. His belief in his own inadequacy fuels his reliance on these rigid control strategies, creating a feedback loop of vigilance, suppression, and deepening despair. His professional identity has begun to crumble under the strain. He feels like a complete fraud, dispensing advice on healing while being fundamentally broken himself. It was this unbearable chasm between his public role and his private reality that finally made him agree with his wife: he could not fix this alone.
